en.title: Biomedical Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What biomedical engineering covers, how degrees are organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What biomedical engineering is
sections.text:
Biomedical engineering is the use of engineering ideas to solve problems in medicine and biology. It covers the design, testing, maintenance and safe use of medical devices, instruments, software, implants and hospital systems. A biomedical engineer needs both engineering skill and a working knowledge of how the body behaves, because a device must fit human anatomy, physiology and clinical practice.

The field is wider than making new machines. It includes clinical engineering, which manages equipment and safety in hospitals, and regulatory work, which shows that a device is safe and effective. It is not medicine: biomedical engineers do not diagnose or treat patients unless they also hold a clinical qualification.

Rules for devices and professional registration differ by country. In Nigeria, COREN, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria, regulates engineering registration. Always check the current law and standards for the country where you will work.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, many universities offer a BEng in biomedical engineering over five years, including industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Some polytechnics offer ND and HND programmes in biomedical engineering technology or a closely related field; entry requirements and progression rules vary. Do not assume one pattern applies everywhere.

In the UK, a BEng usually takes three years and an MEng four; in Scotland each usually takes one year longer. Accreditation is by professional institutions licensed by the Engineering Council. In the United States, a bachelor’s degree usually takes four years, and programmes may be accredited by ABET. A master’s degree commonly takes one to two years and adds advanced courses and a dissertation.

Most programmes end with a final-year project. Professional registration or certification is separate from the degree and has its own requirements.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The introduction stage builds the tools. Engineering mathematics, mechanics, electrical circuits and electronics, chemistry, cell biology and physiology, biochemistry, materials science, computing, numerical methods and statistics all support later work. Physiology is not background reading; it explains what a device must measure or replace.

The core stage applies those tools. Biomechanics and tissue mechanics describe forces in the body. Biofluid mechanics covers blood flow and other fluids. Biomaterials and biocompatibility deal with materials in contact with living tissue. Biosignals, instrumentation and sensors cover measurement. Medical imaging and image processing cover seeing inside the body. Biomedical signal processing, physiological modelling and control cover interpretation and automatic control. Medical device design, rehabilitation and assistive technology, clinical engineering and safety, regulation and standards, professional practice and ethics, and research methods lead to the final project.

At master’s level, students go deeper into advanced biomechanics and mechanobiology, advanced signal and image analysis, tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study by linking each engineering method to a body function. When you learn a circuit, ask what signal it might measure. When you learn fluid flow, ask how blood behaves in an artery. Draw the system before you calculate: source, sensor, signal, processing, display and user.

Write units on every line and check whether an answer is reasonable. Practise hand calculations before using software, then use software to explore real data. In laboratories, keep a clear notebook and record calibration and errors. On clinical visits, observe how staff use equipment and what fails in practice.

Read regulations from the official source for your country, not from old notes. Work through past questions and explain answers aloud. Form a small study group for problems that need physiology and engineering together.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make

keyPoints: Biomedical engineering applies engineering to medical and biological problems, including devices, signals, imaging and hospital safety.
Degree length, title and accreditation differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Study physiology alongside engineering, because the body sets the conditions for every design.
Write units, draw the system and check that answers are reasonable before trusting software.
Regulation and professional registration are country-specific; in Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration.
Record your work clearly, because documentation matters in design, testing and clinical use.

en.title: Introduction to biomedical engineering and the healthcare system
en.short: What biomedical engineering is, its subfields, workplaces and the medical device lifecycle.

sections.heading: Definitions
sections.text: Biomedical engineering (BME) applies engineering principles and design to problems in medicine and healthcare. It aims to prevent, diagnose or treat disease, and to rehabilitate patients. Bioengineering is broader: engineering applied to living systems, including agriculture and food; some universities use the two terms as synonyms, so check a programme’s meaning. Clinical engineering is the hospital-based branch that manages medical equipment through selection, maintenance, safety testing and staff training. Medical physics applies physics to medicine, especially imaging and radiotherapy; in many countries it is a separate profession with its own training and registration.

sections.heading: Subfields and work
sections.text: Main subfields include biomechanics, biomaterials, biosignals and instrumentation, medical imaging, signal and image processing, tissue engineering, rehabilitation engineering, clinical engineering and regulatory affairs. Graduates work for device manufacturers, hospitals, universities and research institutes, regulators and start-ups. They work within healthcare systems, which vary: care may be public, private or mixed, organised from primary clinics to specialist hospitals, and paid for by government, insurance or patients themselves. In Nigeria, engineers register with COREN; other countries have their own bodies and codes. Device rules and registration differ by country, so check the current national requirements rather than assuming one system.

sections.heading: Device lifecycle
sections.text: A medical device moves through stages: identifying a clinical need, design, bench (laboratory) testing and, where needed, animal studies, clinical evaluation, regulatory approval, manufacture, hospital use and maintenance, then retirement and safe disposal. A small case: an engineer in a Nigerian hospital notices nurses struggling to check intravenous flow. She defines the need, builds a low-cost sensor, tests its accuracy against a measured volume, seeks approval, trains staff and plans maintenance and disposal. Later courses supply the tools: physiology for the need, materials and mechanics for design, electronics and computing for instrumentation, statistics for testing, and regulatory affairs and ethics for approval.

sections.heading: Course map
sections.text: Foundation courses give the mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and computing that every subfield uses. Core courses then specialise: biomechanics, biomaterials, instrumentation, imaging, clinical engineering and regulation. The final project joins them in one small design or study.

keyPoints: Biomedical engineering applies engineering principles and design to medicine and healthcare, while bioengineering is broader and is sometimes used as a synonym.
Clinical engineering manages medical equipment in hospitals, and medical physics applies physics to imaging and radiotherapy.
Main subfields include biomechanics, biomaterials, instrumentation, imaging, tissue engineering, rehabilitation and regulatory affairs.
A medical device passes from clinical need and design through testing, approval, manufacture, use, maintenance and disposal.
Later courses provide the technical and professional tools needed at each stage of that lifecycle.
Registration and device regulation differ by country; in Nigeria engineers register with COREN, and current rules should be checked.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for biomedical engineering
en.short: Rates, ODE models, matrices, partial derivatives, Fourier series and Laplace transforms for biomedical engineering.

sections.heading: Rates and totals
sections.text: Differentiation gives a rate of change; integration accumulates small changes. If y depends on time t, dy/dt is its rate. The change from t = a to t = b is ∫ₐᵇ (dy/dt) dt = y(b) − y(a). Example: if a dose leaves blood at r(t) = 2t mg per hour, the loss in 3 hours is ∫₀³ 2t dt = [t²]₀³ = 9 mg.

sections.heading: Differential equations
sections.text: A first-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) links a function to its first derivative. The decay model dN/dt = −kN has solution N = N₀e^(−kt), where N₀ is the start, k the rate constant. Its half-life is t½ = ln 2 ÷ k. For k = 0.1 per hour, t½ = 0.693 ÷ 0.1 = 6.93 hours. A second-order ODE m d²x/dt² + c dx/dt + kx = F(t) models damped oscillation; undamped ω = √(k ÷ m). For m = 1 kg and k = 4 N/m, ω = 2 rad/s.

sections.heading: Matrices and partial derivatives
sections.text: A matrix is an array of numbers. An eigenvector x of a square matrix A satisfies Ax = λx, where the eigenvalue λ is a scalar. Find λ from det(A − λI) = 0, where I is the identity matrix. For A = [[3, 1], [0, 2]], the eigenvalues are 3 and 2. A partial derivative measures change in one variable while others stay fixed. For f(x, y) = x²y, ∂f/∂x = 2xy and ∂f/∂y = x².

sections.heading: Fourier and Laplace
sections.text: A Fourier series writes a periodic signal as a sum of sines and cosines: f(t) = a₀/2 + Σ(aₙ cos nωt + bₙ sin nωt). Coefficients measure each frequency. The Laplace transform changes a function of time into a function of s: F(s) = ∫₀∞ f(t)e^(−st) dt. Example: for f(t) = e^(−2t), F(s) = 1 ÷ (s + 2). It turns y′ + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 3 into Y(s) = 3 ÷ (s + 2), so y(t) = 3e^(−2t).

keyPoints: Differentiation gives a rate and integration gives accumulated change: ∫ₐᵇ (dy/dt) dt = y(b) − y(a).
The decay ODE dN/dt = −kN has solution N = N₀e^(−kt) and half-life t½ = ln 2 ÷ k.
The second-order ODE m d²x/dt² + c dx/dt + kx = F(t) models oscillation; undamped natural frequency is ω = √(k ÷ m).
Eigenvalues solve det(A − λI) = 0, and a partial derivative holds the other variables fixed.
A Fourier series represents a periodic signal as a sum of sine and cosine terms.
The Laplace transform F(s) = ∫₀∞ f(t)e^(−st) dt turns linear ODEs into algebra; for example y′ + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 3 gives y = 3e^(−2t).

en.title: Engineering mechanics: statics and dynamics
en.short: Covers vectors, forces, moments, equilibrium, friction, centroids, motion, energy and impulse for levers and device supports.

sections.heading: Forces and moments
sections.text: Statics studies bodies at rest. A vector has size and direction; force is a vector in newtons (N). Add forces by components. A moment is a force’s turning effect about a point: M = Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance to the force line. Its unit is the newton metre (N·m). A particle is in equilibrium when ΣF = 0. A rigid body also needs ΣM = 0 about any point. Free-body diagrams show every external force and reaction.

sections.heading: Friction and areas
sections.text: Friction opposes sliding. Static friction can rise to Fmax = μsN, where μs is the coefficient of static friction and N is the normal force; kinetic friction is roughly μkN. The centroid is an area’s centre. The second moment of area I measures how area is spread from an axis and resists bending: I = ∫ y² dA. For a rectangle of breadth b and depth d about its centroidal axis, I = bd³/12. Depth raises I.

sections.heading: Motion and kinetics
sections.text: Kinematics describes motion without forces. For constant acceleration a: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as. Kinetics links motion to force: F = ma. Work is force times displacement along the force; it changes kinetic energy, KE = ½mv². Impulse is force times time, and equals change in momentum: Ft = mv − mu.

sections.heading: Biomedical applications
sections.text: Bones act as levers: a joint is the fulcrum, muscle force is the effort and a load is the resistance. Example: a forearm holds a 50 N load 0.30 m from the elbow. A muscle pulls 0.05 m from the elbow. Taking moments about the elbow: F × 0.05 = 50 × 0.30 = 15 N·m, so F = 300 N. The muscle force is larger because its lever arm is shorter. Supports for scanners, beds and drip stands need equilibrium, stable reactions and adequate sections. Design rules differ by country; check the current local code and use a qualified engineer.

keyPoints: Equilibrium of a particle needs ΣF = 0; a rigid body also needs ΣM = 0.
Moment M = Fd, with d measured perpendicular to the force line.
Static friction has a limit Fmax = μsN; kinetic friction is about μkN.
For a rectangle about its centroidal axis, I = bd³/12.
Kinetics uses F = ma; for constant acceleration, v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as.
Work-energy uses KE = ½mv²; impulse-momentum uses Ft = mv − mu.

en.title: Electrical circuits and basic electronics
en.short: Charge, Ohm’s and Kirchhoff’s laws, networks, transients, AC impedance, diodes, op-amps and instruments.

sections.heading: Charge and power
sections.text:
Charge Q is measured in coulombs (C). Current I is the rate of charge flow, I = Q ÷ t, in amperes (A). Voltage V is energy per unit charge, in volts (V). Power P = VI = I²R = V² ÷ R, in watts (W). Ohm’s law, V = IR, holds for a resistor at constant temperature.

Example: a 3 kΩ resistor has 12 V across it.
I = 12 ÷ 3000 = 0.004 A = 4 mA
P = 12 × 0.004 = 0.048 W = 48 mW

sections.heading: Networks and equivalents
sections.text:
Kirchhoff’s current law says currents into a node equal currents out. Kirchhoff’s voltage law says voltages around a closed loop sum to zero. Resistances in series add. For parallel resistors, 1 ÷ R = 1 ÷ R1 + 1 ÷ R2 + ...

Thevenin’s theorem replaces a linear two-terminal network by a voltage source Vth in series with Rth. The Norton equivalent is a current source IN in parallel with RN, where RN = Rth and IN = Vth ÷ Rth.

sections.heading: Capacitors and AC
sections.text:
A capacitor stores charge Q = CV. Its current is i = C dv/dt. An inductor has v = L di/dt. In DC transients, the RC time constant is τ = RC and the RL time constant is τ = L ÷ R.

Phasors represent sine waves as complex amplitudes. Impedance Z = R + jX. A capacitor has impedance 1 ÷ (jωC); an inductor has impedance jωL, where ω = 2πf. Series impedances add.

sections.heading: Diodes and instruments
sections.text:
A diode conducts when forward biased above its threshold voltage and blocks in reverse. An ideal op-amp has high input impedance and low output impedance. With negative feedback, an inverting amplifier has gain −Rf ÷ Rin; a non-inverting amplifier has gain 1 + Rf ÷ Rg.

A multimeter measures voltage in parallel, current in series and resistance with power off. An oscilloscope plots voltage against time.

keyPoints: Current is charge flow, I = Q ÷ t, and power is P = VI = I²R = V² ÷ R.
Ohm’s law is V = IR; series resistances add and parallel conductances add.
Kirchhoff’s laws conserve charge and energy; Thevenin and Norton replace a linear network by Vth with Rth or IN with RN, where IN = Vth ÷ Rth.
For capacitors i = C dv/dt and τ = RC; for inductors v = L di/dt and τ = L ÷ R.
AC impedance is Z = R + jX, with capacitor impedance 1 ÷ (jωC) and inductor impedance jωL.
With negative feedback, op-amp gains are −Rf ÷ Rin and 1 + Rf ÷ Rg; a multimeter goes in parallel for voltage and series for current, and an oscilloscope plots voltage against time.

en.title: General and organic chemistry
en.short: Covers atomic structure, bonding, forces, solutions, pH and buffers, rates, equilibrium and organic groups.

sections.heading: Atomic structure and bonding
sections.text: Atoms contain protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons in orbitals. Atomic number Z is the proton count; mass number A is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes share Z but differ in A. Ionic bonding transfers electrons, covalent bonding shares electron pairs, and metallic bonding has delocalised electrons. Electronegativity is the pull of an atom on shared electrons; unequal pull makes a polar bond.

sections.heading: Forces, states and solutions
sections.text:
Intermolecular forces act between molecules: London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding. They are weaker than covalent bonds but control boiling point, solubility and protein shape. States of matter depend on thermal motion against these forces: solids keep shape, liquids flow, gases fill the container.

A solution is a solute in a solvent. Molarity c = n ÷ V, with n in moles and V in litres. Example: 0.050 mol glucose in 0.250 L gives c = 0.050 ÷ 0.250 = 0.20 mol/L.

sections.heading: Acids, bases and pH
sections.text: A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton (H+); a base accepts one. Strong acids ionise completely; weak acids only partly. pH = −log10[H+], so [H+] = 1.0 × 10−3 mol/L gives pH = 3.00. A buffer is a weak acid with its conjugate base. It resists pH change on adding small amounts of acid or base. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log10([A−] ÷ [HA]). If pKa = 4.76 and [A−] = [HA], pH = 4.76. Rates increase with concentration and temperature; catalysts speed them. Equilibrium is dynamic: forward and reverse rates are equal.

sections.heading: Organic groups and reactions
sections.text: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds. Functional groups give characteristic reactions: hydroxyl (−OH), carbonyl (C=O), carboxyl (−COOH), amino (−NH2), ester and amide. Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures; structural, geometric (cis-trans) and optical isomers exist. Main reaction types are addition, substitution, elimination, condensation, hydrolysis and oxidation-reduction. Amino acids join by condensation into peptide amide bonds; sugars carry hydroxyl and carbonyl groups; fats are esters. Medical polymers such as poly(lactic acid) have ester links that hydrolyse slowly.

keyPoints: Molarity is moles of solute divided by litres of solution: c = n ÷ V.
pH = −log10[H+], and a buffer resists pH change; pH = pKa + log10([A−] ÷ [HA]).
Intermolecular forces are weaker than covalent bonds but control boiling point, solubility and molecular shape.
Reaction rates increase with concentration and temperature, and catalysts speed them; equilibrium is dynamic.
Functional groups such as hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, amino, ester and amide determine organic reactions.
Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in structure; addition, substitution, condensation and hydrolysis are key reaction types.

en.title: Cell biology and human physiology for engineers
en.short: Cell structure, transport, membrane potentials, tissues and system quantities for engineers.

sections.heading: Cells and transport
sections.text: A cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and, in eukaryotes, organelles such as the nucleus and mitochondria. The membrane is a lipid bilayer with proteins and is selectively permeable. Diffusion moves solutes down a concentration gradient; osmosis moves water. Facilitated diffusion uses carrier or channel proteins. Active transport uses energy, often ATP, against a gradient; the sodium-potassium pump is an example. The cell cycle is G1, S, G2 and M; S is DNA replication and M is mitosis.

sections.heading: Electrical signals
sections.text: Excitable cells maintain a resting membrane potential, inside negative, set mainly by potassium leak and the sodium-potassium pump. The Nernst equation gives an ion’s equilibrium potential, the voltage at which that ion has no net flow across the membrane: E = (RT ÷ zF) ln([ion]out ÷ [ion]in). At 37 °C, for a monovalent cation, this is about 61.5 log10([out] ÷ [in]) mV. Example: potassium outside 4 mmol/L and inside 140 mmol/L gives E = 61.5 log10(4 ÷ 140) = −95 mV. An action potential is a rapid change: sodium channels open, the membrane depolarises, then potassium channels restore it.

sections.heading: Tissues and systems
sections.text: Four basic tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue. Epithelium covers and lines surfaces; connective tissue supports and binds; muscle contracts; nervous tissue conducts signals. Systems: cardiovascular (heart, vessels), respiratory (lungs, gas exchange), nervous (sensory and control), musculoskeletal (bones, muscles), renal (kidneys, filtration) and endocrine (hormones). Engineers measure pressure, flow, voltage, volume and concentration, for example blood pressure in mmHg, blood flow in L/min, membrane voltage in mV, lung volume in L, and glucose in mmol/L.

sections.heading: Measured quantities
sections.text: Pressure is force per area (Pa; clinical blood pressure often mmHg). Flow is volume per time (m³/s or L/min). Voltage is potential difference (V or mV). Volume is space occupied (L or mL). Concentration is amount per volume (mol/m³ or mmol/L). Case: blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, heart rate 70 beats/min, stroke volume (blood pumped per beat) 70 mL. Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 70 × 70 = 4,900 mL/min = 4.9 L/min. Actual values vary.

keyPoints: The plasma membrane is a selectively permeable lipid bilayer; diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion and active transport move substances across it.
The Nernst equation E = (RT ÷ zF) ln([ion]out ÷ [ion]in) gives an ion’s equilibrium potential; at 37 °C a monovalent cation follows about 61.5 log10([out] ÷ [in]) mV.
Resting membrane potential is inside negative; an action potential is a rapid depolarisation and repolarisation.
The four basic tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue.
Engineers measure pressure, flow, voltage, volume and concentration; cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
The cell cycle is G1, S, G2 and M, with DNA replication in S and mitosis in M.

en.title: Biochemistry and molecular biology
en.short: Covers amino acids, proteins, enzymes, carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids, metabolism and biomedical uses.

sections.heading: Molecules of life
sections.text:
Biochemistry studies molecules of living systems. Amino acids have amino and carboxyl groups; about twenty standard amino acids link by peptide bonds to form proteins. Carbohydrates are sugars and polymers such as starch and cellulose, used for energy and structure. Lipids are fats, oils and membrane components; they store energy and form barriers. Nucleic acids, DNA and RNA, are chains of nucleotides that store and copy genetic information.

These molecules guide biomedical design. Biosensors may use enzymes or antibodies to recognise targets. Biomaterials may present protein or carbohydrate cues to cells. Tissue engineering scaffolds aim to mimic the extracellular matrix.

sections.heading: Proteins and enzymes
sections.text:
Protein function follows structure. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence; secondary structure includes alpha helices and beta sheets; tertiary structure is the folded three-dimensional shape; quaternary structure is the assembly of subunits. Denaturation destroys function.

Enzymes speed reactions by lowering activation energy. The Michaelis-Menten model is v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]), where [S] is substrate concentration, Vmax is the maximum rate and Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax.

Example: Vmax = 100 µmol/min, Km = 5 mM, [S] = 10 mM. Then v = 100 × 10 ÷ (5 + 10) = 66.7 µmol/min.

sections.heading: DNA and energy
sections.text: DNA replication copies DNA before cell division. Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template. Translation uses mRNA, ribosomes and tRNA to build a protein. ATP is the main energy currency; hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases energy. Core pathways include glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. These pathways release energy from fuels and conserve it as ATP.

sections.heading: Engineering links
sections.text: Engineers use these ideas in biosensors, biomaterials and tissue engineering. Glucose biosensors often use glucose oxidase, an enzyme whose kinetics set the sensor response. Biocompatibility depends partly on how proteins adsorb onto a surface. Scaffold design considers cell adhesion proteins and the supply of oxygen and nutrients.

keyPoints: Amino acids link by peptide bonds to form proteins, and protein function depends on folded three-dimensional structure.
Enzymes lower activation energy, and the Michaelis-Menten model is v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]).
Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax, and Vmax is the maximum reaction rate.
DNA replication copies DNA, transcription makes RNA, and translation builds proteins.
ATP is the main energy currency; core pathways include glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.
Enzyme kinetics and surface proteins guide biosensor, biomaterial and scaffold design.

en.title: Materials science fundamentals
en.short: Crystal structure, defects, mechanical properties, phase diagrams, ceramics, polymers, composites and corrosion.

sections.heading: Atomic packing and defects
sections.text:
In many solids, atoms pack in regular patterns. The atomic packing factor is the fraction of space filled by atoms. Crystal structures include body-centred cubic, face-centred cubic and hexagonal close-packed; glasses are amorphous.

Crystals contain point defects such as vacancies, line defects called dislocations, and grain boundaries. Diffusion is atom movement driven by a concentration gradient. Fick’s first law is J = −D dC/dx, where J is flux, D is diffusivity and dC/dx is the gradient. Diffusion is important in heat treatment and corrosion.

sections.heading: Mechanical behaviour
sections.text:
A tensile test plots stress against strain. Stress σ = F ÷ A, strain ε = ΔL ÷ L, and Young’s modulus E = σ ÷ ε in the elastic region. Yield strength marks the start of plastic deformation; ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress; ductility is strain before fracture.

Hardness is resistance to local indentation. Fatigue is failure under repeated stress. Creep is slow deformation under sustained load at high temperature. Example: a 100 mm specimen stretches 0.10 mm. ε = 0.10 ÷ 100 = 0.001. If σ = 200 MPa, E = 200 ÷ 0.001 = 200,000 MPa = 200 GPa.

sections.heading: Phases and heat treatment
sections.text:
A phase diagram shows stable phases at given temperature and composition. The eutectic point is where a liquid solidifies into two solid phases.

Heat treatment uses controlled heating and cooling to change microstructure. Annealing softens and removes stress; quenching hardens steel; tempering reduces brittleness. Exact temperatures and times depend on the alloy and must come from the supplier or standard.

sections.heading: Materials and selection
sections.text:
Ceramics are hard and brittle and resist heat and wear. Polymers are long-chain molecules, light and flexible, but soften at lower temperatures. Composites combine two materials, such as fibres in a matrix, to get properties neither has alone.

Corrosion is electrochemical degradation of metals; polymers may degrade by ultraviolet light, heat or hydrolysis. Material selection uses property charts, such as strength against density, to compare candidates. The final choice must meet the standard.

keyPoints: Atomic packing factor is the fraction of space filled by atoms; common structures are BCC, FCC and HCP.
Point defects, dislocations and grain boundaries affect properties; diffusion follows Fick’s first law J = −D dC/dx.
Stress σ = F ÷ A, strain ε = ΔL ÷ L, and Young’s modulus E = σ ÷ ε in the elastic region.
Fatigue is failure under repeated stress; creep is slow deformation under sustained load at high temperature.
Phase diagrams show stable phases; annealing, quenching and tempering change microstructure.
Property charts compare materials, but the final choice must meet the relevant standard and application needs.

en.title: Computing and numerical methods
en.short: Programming basics and numerical methods for roots, fitting, calculus, systems and ODEs.

sections.heading: Programming basics
sections.text: A high-level language such as Python lets you write instructions close to ordinary algebra. A variable is a named store for a value. Control flow chooses between paths (if) or repeats work (for, while). A function packages a calculation so it can be reused and tested. An array holds many values under one name, indexed from zero in Python and many languages. Plotting turns arrays into graphs for checking results. Learn one language well; the ideas transfer.

sections.heading: Roots and fitting
sections.text: Root finding solves f(x)=0. Bisection needs a sign change: if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, a root lies between them. Test the midpoint and keep the half with the sign change. The bracket halves each step, so the error bound halves. Example: f(x)=x²−2 on [1,2]. f(1)=−1, f(2)=2. Midpoint 1.5 gives 0.25, so keep [1,1.5]. Midpoint 1.25 gives −0.4375, so keep [1.25,1.5]. Midpoint 1.375 gives −0.109375, so keep [1.375,1.5]. The root √2 ≈ 1.414 lies there. Interpolation estimates between known points; curve fitting finds a model, often by least squares, which minimises squared errors.

sections.heading: Calculus and systems
sections.text: Numerical integration approximates area under a curve. The trapezoidal rule with equally spaced points is ∫ f(x) dx ≈ h/2 [f0 + 2f1 + 2f2 + ... + 2f_{n−1} + fn], where h is spacing. Numerical differentiation uses small differences, for example f′(x) ≈ [f(x+h) − f(x−h)] ÷ (2h). Linear systems Ax = b are solved by elimination or iterative methods. Simple differential equations can be stepped forward with Euler’s method: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n). Small h improves accuracy but costs time.

sections.heading: Reproducible work
sections.text: Data handling matters as much as the method. Keep raw data unchanged, record units, and script every step rather than editing by hand. Store code and data together, use version control, and set random seeds. Check a numerical result by refining the step size or comparing with an exact case. Report the method, inputs and software version so another person can repeat the work.

keyPoints: A variable stores a value; control flow selects or repeats steps; functions and arrays make calculations reusable and testable.
Bisection needs a sign change and halves the root bracket each step.
Least squares curve fitting minimises squared residuals; linear systems Ax = b are solved by elimination or iteration.
Trapezoidal rule: ∫ f(x) dx ≈ h/2 [f0 + 2f1 + 2f2 + ... + 2f_{n−1} + fn].
Central difference: f′(x) ≈ [f(x+h) − f(x−h)] ÷ (2h); Euler step: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n).
Reproducible work keeps raw data, scripts, units, seeds and software versions.

en.title: Probability, statistics and data analysis
en.short: Describing data, probability models, sampling, confidence intervals, tests, regression and design.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise a sample. The mean is the sum divided by n. The median is the middle value in ordered data. The sample standard deviation s measures spread: s = √(Σ(x − xbar)² ÷ (n − 1)); the variance is s².

A histogram shows shape, skew and outliers. Always report units and n.

sections.heading: Probability models
sections.text:
The binomial distribution counts successes in n independent trials with probability p: P(X = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1 − p)^(n−k). The Poisson distribution counts rare events in a fixed interval with mean λ: P(X = k) = e^(−λ) λ^k ÷ k!.

The normal distribution is the bell curve with mean μ and standard deviation σ. Standardise with z = (x − μ) ÷ σ. Check that data are roughly normal before using normal methods.

sections.heading: Sampling and tests
sections.text:
The central limit theorem says the mean of a random sample is approximately normal when n is large. The standard error of a mean is SE = s ÷ √n. A 95% confidence interval is xbar +/- t × SE, with t from the t distribution (n − 1 degrees of freedom).

Example: readings 120, 130, 125, 135, 140 give mean 130 and s = 7.91. SE = 7.91 ÷ √5 = 3.54. With t = 2.776, the interval is 130 +/- 9.82, or 120.18 to 139.82.

A hypothesis test compares a statistic with a null distribution and gives a p-value. Use a t-test for one or two means, chi-square for category counts, and ANOVA for three or more means.

sections.heading: Relations and design
sections.text:
Correlation r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables, from −1 to +1. Linear regression fits y = a + bx, where b = Σ((x − xbar)(y − ybar)) ÷ Σ(x − xbar)² and a = ybar − b xbar.

Experiments use randomisation, replication, blocking and a control group. Software R, Python, SPSS or Stata handles these calculations; learn to check assumptions and read output.

keyPoints: Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − xbar)² ÷ (n − 1)).
Binomial P(X = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1 − p)^(n−k); Poisson P(X = k) = e^(−λ) λ^k ÷ k!.
For a normal variable, z = (x − μ) ÷ σ; the central limit theorem makes the sample mean roughly normal for large n.
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n; a 95% confidence interval for a mean is xbar +/- t × SE.
Use t-tests for one or two means, chi-square for category counts, and ANOVA for three or more means.
Correlation r runs from −1 to +1; regression y = a + bx with b = Σ((x − xbar)(y − ybar)) ÷ Σ(x − xbar)² and a = ybar − b xbar.

en.title: Biomechanics of human movement
en.short: Gait, joint kinetics, muscle mechanics, levers, balance and motion measurement.

sections.heading: Anatomy and gait
sections.text: Bones act as levers and joints as bearings. Hinge joints such as the knee and elbow allow one main rotation; ball-and-socket joints such as the hip and shoulder allow three. Engineers describe this as degrees of freedom. The gait cycle runs from one heel strike to the next heel strike of the same foot. In normal walking, stance takes about 60% of the cycle and swing about 40%, though this varies. Step length is the distance between opposite feet; stride length is one full cycle, or two steps. Cadence is steps per minute.

sections.heading: Kinetics and inverse dynamics
sections.text:
A force plate measures ground reaction force (GRF) in three directions and the centre of pressure. A joint moment is force × perpendicular moment arm. Inverse dynamics combines measured motion (positions, velocities and accelerations) with segment masses and inertias from anthropometric tables and the GRF. It solves the Newton-Euler equations for the net joint force and moment. It gives the net moment, not individual muscle forces.

Example: a 100 N load held 0.30 m from the elbow creates 100 × 0.30 = 30 N·m. If the biceps acts at 0.04 m, the muscle force needed is 30 ÷ 0.04 = 750 N.

sections.heading: Muscle and levers
sections.text: The force-length relation says active muscle force is greatest at an optimum length and falls when the muscle is shorter or longer. The force-velocity relation says force falls as shortening speed rises (concentric action) and rises during forced lengthening (eccentric action). Most limb muscles act as third-class levers: the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load. Mechanical advantage is effort arm ÷ load arm, so it is below one. This trades force for speed and range of motion.

sections.heading: Balance and measurement
sections.text: Balance requires the centre of mass to stay over the base of support. Motion capture with skin markers and force plates feeds the inverse dynamics pipeline. Applications include prosthetic alignment and energy-storing feet, ankle-foot orthoses, and injury analysis such as anterior cruciate ligament loading. Marker placement and soft-tissue movement cause measurement error.

keyPoints: In normal walking, stance is about 60% of the gait cycle and swing about 40%, but values vary.
Joint moment = force × perpendicular moment arm; inverse dynamics solves Newton-Euler equations for net joint moments.
Active muscle force peaks at optimum length (force-length relation).
Concentric force falls as shortening speed rises; eccentric force rises (force-velocity relation).
Most musculoskeletal levers are third class, so mechanical advantage is below one.
A 100 N load at 0.30 m gives 30 N·m; with a 0.04 m moment arm, muscle force is 750 N.

en.title: Tissue mechanics and viscoelasticity
en.short: Stress, strain, anisotropy and viscoelastic models for biological tissues and their testing.

sections.heading: Stress and strain
sections.text:
Stress is force divided by area. Strain is change in length divided by original length. A constitutive equation links stress to strain for a material. Most biological tissues are anisotropic: their properties depend on direction. They are also nonlinear: stiffness usually rises as strain increases, partly because collagen fibres straighten and share load.

Example: a tendon 100 mm long and 10 mm² in cross-section carries 20 N and extends 1 mm.
Stress = 20 N ÷ 10 mm² = 2 N/mm² = 2 MPa.
Strain = 1 mm ÷ 100 mm = 0.01.
If it behaved linearly over this range, E = stress ÷ strain = 2 MPa ÷ 0.01 = 200 MPa. Real tendons are nonlinear, so this is a secant modulus, not a constant.

sections.heading: Viscoelastic models
sections.text:
Viscoelastic materials respond to both load and time. Creep is increasing strain under constant stress. Stress relaxation is falling stress under constant strain. Hysteresis is the energy lost in a load-unload cycle.

A dashpot is a piston moving in viscous fluid.
The Maxwell model is a spring and dashpot in series. It relaxes stress but shows steady creep. The Kelvin-Voigt model places them in parallel; it shows creep but no instantaneous elastic strain and no stress relaxation. The standard linear solid adds a third element, so it can show both creep and relaxation. These are one-dimensional idealisations; real tissues need direction-dependent, nonlinear forms.

sections.heading: Poroelasticity and tissues
sections.text:
Poroelasticity describes a porous solid filled with fluid. Load raises fluid pressure; fluid flows out slowly, so deformation is time-dependent. Cartilage behaves this way and uses fluid pressurisation to carry load.

Bone is stiff and anisotropic, strongest along its long axis. Cartilage is soft in compression and poroelastic. Tendon and ligament are nonlinear and viscoelastic, with collagen aligned along load. Skin is anisotropic and viscoelastic. Blood vessels are anisotropic, viscoelastic and pre-stressed. Common tests are tensile, compression, shear and indentation tests, plus creep and relaxation tests. Values vary widely with site, age, species and test method.

keyPoints: Stress = force ÷ area and strain = change in length ÷ original length; for a linear elastic material E = stress ÷ strain.
Biological tissues are usually anisotropic and nonlinear, so a single elastic modulus is only an approximation over a limited range.
Maxwell model: spring and dashpot in series; it predicts stress relaxation and steady creep.
Kelvin-Voigt model: spring and dashpot in parallel; it predicts creep but no instantaneous elastic strain or stress relaxation.
Standard linear solid adds a third element and can reproduce both creep and stress relaxation; hysteresis is energy loss per cycle.
Poroelasticity explains time-dependent deformation in fluid-filled tissues such as cartilage; properties vary with direction, site, age and test method.

en.title: Biofluid mechanics
en.short: Fluid properties, Poiseuille flow, Reynolds number, pulsatile flow, Windkessel and blood rheology.

sections.heading: Fluid properties and conservation
sections.text: Blood and air are fluids: they deform continuously under shear. Density ρ is mass per volume; dynamic viscosity μ resists shear, and kinematic viscosity ν = μ ÷ ρ. Hydrostatic pressure rises with depth: ΔP = ρgΔh. For steady incompressible flow in a tube, continuity gives A₁V₁ = A₂V₂. Bernoulli relates pressure, speed and height along a streamline: P + ½ρV² + ρgh = constant, but it assumes steady, inviscid, incompressible flow. The Navier-Stokes equations add viscous forces and acceleration; they are Newton’s second law for a fluid element.

sections.heading: Viscous flow and Reynolds number
sections.text: Poiseuille flow is steady, laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian fluid in a circular tube. Q = πΔP R⁴ ÷ (8μL), so flow is very sensitive to radius. Reynolds number Re = ρVD ÷ μ (or VD ÷ ν) compares inertia with viscosity. Pipe flow becomes turbulent at roughly Re ≈ 2000, though the exact value depends on disturbance and geometry. Turbulence increases mixing and pressure loss. Example: R = 2 mm, L = 0.1 m, ΔP = 100 Pa, μ = 0.0035 Pa·s. Q = π × 100 × (0.002)⁴ ÷ (8 × 0.0035 × 0.1) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ m³/s, about 1.8 mL/s.

sections.heading: Pulsatile flow and Windkessel
sections.text: Arterial flow is pulsatile. The Womersley number α = R√(ω ÷ ν) compares unsteady inertia with viscous effects; ω is angular frequency. Low α gives a nearly parabolic velocity profile; high α gives a flatter profile with phase lag. The Windkessel model treats arteries as a compliance C and peripheral resistance R; pressure decays with time constant τ = RC. Blood is non-Newtonian: shear-thinning at low shear, nearly Newtonian at high shear.

sections.heading: Airways, valves and measurement
sections.text: In airways, branching and compliance affect resistance; Poiseuille flow applies only to slow laminar regions. Through heart valves flow is often inertial and turbulent, so pressure drop rises with velocity squared. Pressure is measured with catheters and transducers; flow with ultrasonic Doppler, electromagnetic or thermal sensors. Calibration and correct zeroing matter.

keyPoints: Continuity for steady incompressible flow is A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, and hydrostatic pressure rises as ΔP = ρgΔh.
Bernoulli: P + ½ρV² + ρgh = constant for steady inviscid flow; the Navier-Stokes equations add viscosity and acceleration.
Poiseuille flow: Q = πΔP R⁴ ÷ (8μL), so small changes in radius greatly change flow.
Reynolds number Re = ρVD ÷ μ; high Re indicates turbulence, roughly above 2000 in pipe flow but the transition varies.
Womersley number α = R√(ω ÷ ν) compares pulsatile inertia with viscosity; the Windkessel model gives pressure decay τ = RC.
Blood is shear-thinning at low shear and nearly Newtonian at high shear; valve and airway flows can be turbulent, so sensors need calibration.

en.title: Biomaterials and biocompatibility
en.short: Classes of biomaterials, their degradation and wear, host response, sterilisation and ISO 10993 testing.

sections.heading: Material classes
sections.text:
A biomaterial is a material used in contact with living tissue to treat, replace or support a body function. Metals (316L stainless steel, cobalt-chromium, titanium alloys) are strong and tough but can corrode. Ceramics (alumina, zirconia, hydroxyapatite) are hard, wear resistant and often brittle.

Polymers (polyethylene, acrylic bone cement, silicone and polylactic acid) are flexible and easy to shape. Composites combine phases, such as carbon fibre in a polymer. Natural materials include collagen, chitosan and alginate.

sections.heading: Bulk and surface
sections.text:
Bulk properties (elastic modulus, strength, fatigue life) carry load. Surface properties (chemistry, roughness, wettability) control protein adsorption and cell attachment.

Degradation is breakdown by hydrolysis, oxidation or enzymes; corrosion is electrochemical attack on metals; wear is loss of material by rubbing. Wear particles can trigger inflammation and bone loss.

sections.heading: Biocompatibility
sections.text:
Biocompatibility is the ability of a material to perform its function without causing an unacceptable host response. Blood contact can cause thrombosis: platelets adhere and the clotting cascade activates.

Infection often begins as a biofilm, a layer of bacteria on the surface. Host response runs from protein adsorption through inflammation to a fibrous capsule.

sections.heading: Selection and testing
sections.text:
Selection matches bulk and surface properties to the device, its load, its duration and its sterilisation. Moist heat autoclaving suits metals and some heat-tolerant polymers but damages many others; ethylene oxide, gamma irradiation and plasma are alternatives. The ISO 10993 series sets a risk-based framework for biological evaluation, from in vitro cytotoxicity to implantation and haemocompatibility tests. Regulators apply it differently by country.

Case: Ngozi’s team in Ibadan compares a 316L stainless steel bone plate with a titanium alloy plate. Titanium resists corrosion better and has a lower modulus, but costs more.

keyPoints: Biomaterials are metals, ceramics, polymers, composites or natural materials chosen for bulk and surface properties.
Biocompatibility means the material performs its function without an unacceptable host response.
Corrosion, wear and degradation release products that can cause inflammation and implant loosening.
Blood-contacting devices can trigger thrombosis; infection often involves biofilm.
Sterilisation must suit the material; autoclave, ethylene oxide, gamma and plasma are common methods.
ISO 10993 gives a risk-based framework for biological evaluation, applied by national regulators.

en.title: Biosignals and physiological measurement
en.short: How bioelectric signals arise, how electrodes and amplifiers record them, and how to read traces.

sections.heading: Signal origins
sections.text:
Bioelectric signals arise from ion movement across cell membranes. Resting cells have a membrane potential; stimulation changes ion-channel permeability and produces action potentials.

ECG records summed heart activity, EEG the brain, EMG skeletal muscle, and EOG the eye, which acts as a dipole. Evoked potentials are small responses time-locked to a stimulus such as a flash or click. ECG amplitudes are often millivolts; EEG and evoked potentials are microvolts, so amplification and reference choice matter.

sections.heading: Electrodes and interface
sections.text:
A biopotential electrode converts ionic current in tissue to electronic current in a wire. At the electrode-electrolyte interface a half-cell potential and contact impedance appear; Ag/AgCl electrodes with gel are common because they are stable and low-noise. Prepare skin, use good contact, and allow settling.

The amplifier should be differential, with high input impedance, high common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) and suitable bandwidth. Filters reduce drift and noise; choose cut-offs that keep wanted content. Example: differential gain 1000, common-mode gain 0.5, so CMRR = 1000 ÷ 0.5 = 2000, or 20 log10(2000) ≈ 66 dB.

sections.heading: Safety and artefacts
sections.text:
Patient safety comes first. Use an isolation amplifier and limit leakage current; exact limits and device rules differ by country, so check the current national standard and regulator. Professional registration also differs, for example COREN in Nigeria.

Common artefacts are motion, muscle activity, powerline interference and baseline wander. Check electrodes, reduce movement, and filter only when wanted content is not removed. Record a calibration signal and note gain, filter settings and lead placement.

sections.heading: Reading waveforms
sections.text:
Display signals with known time base and voltage scale. Identify timing landmarks: P, QRS and T waves in ECG; alpha rhythm in EEG; bursts in EMG; step changes in EOG.

In the laboratory, calibrate, record a quiet baseline, then ask the subject to perform a defined task and repeat trials. Interpret only with recording conditions known; a single trace is not a diagnosis. Evoked potentials are averaged over repeats to raise the small response above noise.

keyPoints: Bioelectric signals arise from ion movement and action potentials; ECG, EEG, EMG, EOG and evoked potentials differ in source, amplitude and frequency.
A biopotential electrode converts ionic current to electronic current; the electrode-electrolyte interface adds half-cell potential and contact impedance.
A good biopotential amplifier is differential with high input impedance and high CMRR; CMRR = differential gain ÷ common-mode gain.
Filters reduce baseline drift and high-frequency noise, but must not remove wanted signal content.
Patient safety requires isolation and leakage-current control; limits and registration differ by country, so check the current national standard and regulator.
Calibrate, label gain, filter and lead settings, and average evoked potentials; a single trace is not a diagnosis.

en.title: Biomedical instrumentation and sensors
en.short: Measurement chain, sensors, bridge conditioning, ADC, calibration and testing of biomedical instruments.

sections.heading: Measurement chain
sections.text: A biomedical instrument converts a physical or chemical quantity into a reading. The measurement chain is sensor, signal conditioning, analogue-to-digital converter (ADC), processor and display. The sensor responds to the quantity. Conditioning amplifies, filters and converts the signal. The ADC samples it. The display shows the result. Each stage adds error, so the weakest stage limits performance.

sections.heading: Sensors
sections.text: Pressure sensors use a diaphragm with strain gauges or capacitance. Flow sensors use ultrasonic transit time, electromagnetic induction or thermal transport. Temperature sensors include thermistors, resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) and thermocouples. Force often uses a load cell, a strain-gauged elastic element. Displacement uses a linear variable differential transformer (LVDT), potentiometer or capacitance. Chemical sensors include electrochemical cells, ion-selective electrodes and optical sensors. A pH electrode responds to hydrogen ion activity.

sections.heading: Conditioning and ADC
sections.text:
Bridge circuits turn small resistance changes into voltage. For a quarter bridge with one active gauge, Vout ≈ Vs × ΔR ÷ (4R). An instrumentation amplifier rejects shared noise. A filter limits noise and prevents aliasing, where sampling too slowly makes fast signals appear as false slow ones. An n-bit ADC has 2^n levels, so resolution = range ÷ 2^n.

Example: R = 350 Ω, gauge factor 2, strain 500 microstrain, Vs = 5 V.
ΔR = 350 × 2 × 500 × 10^-6 = 0.35 Ω
Vout = 5 × 0.35 ÷ (4 × 350) = 1.25 mV
A 12-bit ADC over 0 to 5 V has resolution 5 ÷ 4096 = 1.22 mV.

sections.heading: Calibration and testing
sections.text: Calibration compares readings with a known standard and gives a calibration curve. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is repeatability. Error = measured value − true value. Drift is slow change over time or temperature. Test a small system by checking each stage, then the whole chain against known inputs. Record sensitivity, offset, linearity and noise. Limits and registration rules differ by country; check the current official source.

keyPoints: Measurement chain: sensor, conditioning, ADC, processor, display.
Quarter bridge output is Vout ≈ Vs × ΔR ÷ (4R).
An n-bit ADC has 2^n levels; resolution = range ÷ 2^n.
Calibration compares readings with a known standard.
Accuracy is closeness to truth; precision is repeatability.
Drift is slow change with time or temperature; test each stage and the whole chain.

en.title: Medical imaging modalities
en.short: Physical principles, image formation, resolution, dose and safety of the main medical imaging methods.

sections.heading: X-ray and CT
sections.text:
X-rays are ionising photons. A tube accelerates electrons into a metal target; tissue attenuates the beam by photoelectric absorption and Compton scattering. Contrast depends on the linear attenuation coefficient μ, which rises with density and atomic number. Transmission follows I = I0 e−μx. If μ = 0.10 mm⁻¹ and x = 10 mm, I/I0 = e−1 = 0.37.

CT reconstructs slices from many projections, often by filtered back projection or iterative methods. CT numbers are H = 1000(μ − μwater)/μwater; water is 0 HU, air −1000 HU.

sections.heading: Ultrasound and MRI
sections.text:
Ultrasound uses pulsed sound. A transducer emits and receives echoes; depth is d = ct/2, with c ≈ 1540 m/s and t echo time. For t = 26 µs, d = 1540 × 26×10⁻⁶ ÷ 2 = 0.020 m = 2.0 cm. Contrast comes from acoustic impedance mismatches; higher frequency improves resolution but reduces penetration.

MRI uses nuclear magnetic resonance of hydrogen protons in a strong field. Radiofrequency pulses excite spins; gradients encode position; Fourier methods reconstruct the image. It gives high soft-tissue contrast without ionising radiation.

sections.heading: Nuclear and optical
sections.text:
Nuclear medicine uses a radiotracer labelled with a gamma-emitting isotope. Gamma cameras image its distribution; PET detects annihilation photons from positron emitters and maps metabolism.

Optical methods use visible or near-infrared light and measure absorption, scattering or fluorescence; light penetrates only millimetres to a few centimetres, so optical imaging is mainly superficial or endoscopic.

sections.heading: Choosing and safety
sections.text:
Resolution is the smallest separable detail; contrast is the signal difference between tissues; noise limits both. X-ray, CT and nuclear medicine use ionising radiation, so justify each exposure and keep dose low. MRI avoids ionising radiation but requires screening for implants and metal. Ultrasound is generally safe but high exposure can heat tissue or cause cavitation.

Choose by the clinical question: X-ray or CT for bone and lung, ultrasound for abdominal and obstetric questions, MRI for soft tissue and brain, nuclear medicine for function, optical for superficial tissue.

keyPoints: X-ray transmission is I = I0 e−μx, and CT numbers are H = 1000(μ − μwater)/μwater.
Ultrasound echo depth is d = ct/2, with c about 1540 m/s in soft tissue.
CT reconstructs from projections; MRI uses radiofrequency excitation, gradients and Fourier reconstruction.
Nuclear medicine images radiotracer distribution, and PET detects annihilation photons.
Resolution, contrast and noise set image quality; ionising modalities require dose justification.

Choose by the clinical question and safety: X-ray or CT for bone and lung, ultrasound for abdomen and obstetrics, MRI for soft tissue and brain, nuclear medicine for function, optical for superficial tissue.

en.title: Image processing and analysis
en.short: Pixels, sampling, enhancement, segmentation, morphology, registration and simple classification.

sections.heading: Digital images
sections.text:
A digital image is a grid of pixels. Each pixel holds an intensity; a grey image is f(x,y), with x and y pixel indices. Sampling fixes grid spacing; quantisation fixes intensity levels, often 8 bits (256 levels). Too few samples blur detail; too few levels create false contours.

Example: a cell has diameter 20 pixels and spacing 0.5 µm/pixel. Radius = 10 pixels. Area = π × 10² = 314.16 pixels². Physical area = 314.16 × 0.5² = 78.54 µm². Diameter = 20 × 0.5 = 10 µm.

sections.heading: Enhancement and filtering
sections.text:
Point operations change each pixel from its value alone: brightness offset, contrast scaling, inversion and thresholding. Histogram processing counts intensity frequencies; histogram equalisation spreads the histogram to use the full range, improving contrast but amplifying noise.

Filtering uses neighbours. A mean filter averages a window, smoothing noise but blurring edges. A Gaussian filter weights nearby pixels more. A median filter replaces a pixel with the window median, removing salt-and-pepper noise while preserving edges. Sharpening adds a scaled edge image.

sections.heading: Edges and morphology
sections.text:
Edge detection finds intensity changes. Sobel operators estimate horizontal and vertical gradients; Canny adds smoothing, non-maximum suppression and hysteresis. Segmentation divides an image into regions. Thresholding is simplest; Otsu chooses a threshold from the histogram. Region growing and watershed handle touching objects.

Morphological operations use a structuring element, a small shape such as a square or disk that is moved over the image. Erosion shrinks bright regions, dilation expands them. Opening (erosion then dilation) removes small specks; closing (dilation then erosion) fills small holes. These help count cells and measure regions.

sections.heading: Registration and practice
sections.text:
Registration aligns images by estimating a transform: translation, rotation, scaling or non-rigid. It is needed for comparing scans over time or across modalities. Simple classification assigns a label from features such as area, shape or intensity; train and test on separate data.

Practical work uses Python with NumPy, scikit-image or OpenCV. Keep pixel spacing, record every step, and validate counts against a manual or phantom standard. Codes and acceptance rules vary by country; check the local regulator.

keyPoints: A digital image is a grid of intensities f(x,y); sampling sets pixel spacing and quantisation sets the number of levels.
Histogram equalisation remaps intensities to spread the histogram, improving contrast but also amplifying noise.
Mean and Gaussian filters smooth noise and blur edges; a median filter removes salt-and-pepper noise while preserving edges.
Sobel estimates gradients; Canny adds smoothing, non-maximum suppression and hysteresis before edge linking.
Erosion shrinks bright regions and dilation expands them; opening removes small specks and closing fills small holes.
Physical length = length in pixels × spacing; physical area = pixel count × spacing².

en.title: Biomedical signal processing
en.short: Sampling, spectra, digital filters, averaging and feature extraction from ECG, EEG and EMG.

sections.heading: Sampling and quantisation
sections.text:
A signal is sampled at fs samples per second. The Nyquist criterion says fs must exceed twice the highest frequency fmax, otherwise higher frequencies fold down as aliases. For example, a 50 Hz tone sampled at 60 Hz appears at |50 − 60| = 10 Hz. An anti-alias low-pass filter before the ADC prevents this.

Quantisation rounds each sample to one of 2^n levels for an n-bit ADC. Step size = range ÷ 2^n; error is at most ± half a step. A 10-bit ADC over 0 to 5 V has step 5 ÷ 1024 = 4.88 mV and maximum error ±2.44 mV.

sections.heading: Frequency domain
sections.text: The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) converts N samples into N frequency bins: X[k] = Σ x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N). Magnitude shows amplitude at each frequency; phase shows timing. Bin spacing is fs ÷ N, so a longer record gives finer resolution. Leakage occurs when the record lacks a whole number of cycles; a Hann window reduces it but widens peaks. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the DFT efficiently.

sections.heading: Digital filters
sections.text:
A moving average filter y[n] = (1/M) Σ x[n − i] smooths a signal and is a simple low-pass filter. A Butterworth filter has a maximally flat passband; its order sets how sharply it cuts. A notch filter removes one narrow band, often 50 Hz or 60 Hz mains interference. Mains frequency varies: Nigeria uses 50 Hz, North America 60 Hz.

Correlation compares signals: autocorrelation finds repeating patterns, cross-correlation finds delay between channels. Ensemble averaging of M aligned repeats reduces uncorrelated random noise by about √M.

sections.heading: ECG, EEG and EMG
sections.text: ECG feature extraction often starts with a band-pass filter, a mains notch and QRS detection by thresholding the filtered signal. EEG analysis uses band powers: delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma, after removing eye and muscle artefacts. EMG features include rectified mean, RMS and median frequency. Filter before measuring amplitude, check that wanted components remain, and validate features on labelled data.

keyPoints: Nyquist criterion: fs > 2fmax; otherwise higher frequencies alias to lower ones.
Quantisation step = range ÷ 2^n, with maximum rounding error ± half a step.
DFT: X[k] = Σ x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N), with frequency spacing fs ÷ N.
A moving average filter is y[n] = (1/M) Σ x[n − i]; a Butterworth filter has a flat passband; a notch filter removes mains interference.
Ensemble averaging of M independent repeats reduces random noise by about √M.
For ECG, EEG and EMG, filter artefacts first, then extract validated time or frequency features.

en.title: Physiological modelling and control
en.short: Compartmental models, transfer functions, feedback and PID, with glucose, drug and ventilation examples.

sections.heading: Compartments and balance
sections.text:
A compartment is a well-mixed pool of a substance. A compartmental model writes a mass balance for each pool: rate of change = input − output. For one compartment with first-order elimination, V dC/dt = −kVC, so C(t) = C₀e^(−kt), where V is volume, k the elimination rate constant and C₀ the starting concentration.

Example: 500 mg into V = 20 L gives C₀ = 500 ÷ 20 = 25 mg/L. With k = 0.1 h⁻¹, half-life = 0.693 ÷ 0.1 = 6.93 h.

sections.heading: Transfer functions
sections.text:
Treating the body as linear and time-invariant allows Laplace transforms. The transfer function G(s) = Y(s) ÷ U(s) relates output to input. A first-order system G(s) = K ÷ (τs + 1) has gain K and time constant τ; after a step it reaches about 63% of its final value in one τ.

State-space form writes the same system as dx/dt = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du, where x is the state vector. It handles several compartments at once.

sections.heading: Feedback and PID
sections.text:
Negative feedback compares measured output with a setpoint and acts on the error e = setpoint − output. Proportional action gives u = Kp e. Integral action removes steady offset; derivative action damps overshoot. Together, u = Kp(e + (1/Ti)∫e dt + Td de/dt).

Stability means the output settles after a disturbance. In a linear model the poles, the roots of the denominator, must have negative real parts. Too much gain can cause oscillation.

sections.heading: Examples and limits
sections.text:
Glucose-insulin models link glucose and insulin compartments; the minimal model estimates insulin sensitivity from a glucose tolerance test. Drug delivery uses one- or two-compartment pharmacokinetics to set dose and interval. Ventilation models relate airway pressure to flow and volume through compliance and resistance.

Parameters are identified by fitting model output to measured data, usually by least squares. Estimates are only as good as the data: noise, unmeasured inputs and nonlinearity limit them. A model is valid only over the range tested.

keyPoints: One-compartment elimination: C(t) = C₀e^(−kt), half-life = 0.693 ÷ k.
First-order transfer function: G(s) = K ÷ (τs + 1), with time constant τ.
State-space form: dx/dt = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du.
PID control: u = Kp(e + (1/Ti)∫e dt + Td de/dt).
A linear system is stable when all poles have negative real parts.
Model parameters are fitted to measured data and are valid only over the range tested.

en.title: Medical device design and development
en.short: Needs finding, specifications, risk analysis, prototyping, verification, validation, usability and design control.

sections.heading: Needs and specifications
sections.text:
Needs finding starts by watching and interviewing users. A team at a Nigerian university, led by Ada and Tunde, sees that rural clinics lack affordable pulse oximeters. The need is a reliable, low-cost device that a nurse can use with little training.

The team writes design inputs: measurable specifications. These include oxygen saturation range 70 to 100 percent, heart rate 30 to 250 beats per minute, battery life of at least 8 hours, a target cost, and a drop test. Each input must be testable.

sections.heading: Risk and concepts
sections.text:
Concept generation produces several candidate designs. Risk analysis identifies hazards and estimates severity and probability. ISO 14971 is the international standard for risk management of medical devices. For the oximeter, hazards include wrong readings from movement, pressure injury from a tight probe, and electrical shock. Mitigations include motion detection, a soft probe, and electrical isolation.

Human factors and usability are part of risk analysis. A device that is hard to use creates use-related hazards. Formative usability tests with nurses find these problems early.

sections.heading: Prototyping and testing
sections.text:
Prototypes move from proof of concept to functional models. Verification checks whether the design meets its specifications. The team tests the oximeter against a calibrated simulator. Validation checks whether the device meets the user need in the intended environment. The team compares readings with a reference oximeter on volunteers and runs a simulated clinic session.

Verification asks did we build the device right; validation asks did we build the right device.

sections.heading: Design control and team
sections.text:
Design control is a documented process linking needs, specifications, design outputs, verification and validation. A design history file holds the records. Design reviews check the work. Change management assesses every change for risk and re-verifies it. Traceability links each specification to a test.

ISO 13485 is the international standard for medical device quality management. Regulators in many countries require design controls. In Nigeria, NAFDAC regulates medical devices and COREN registers engineers. The team project carries a concept to a tested prototype.

keyPoints: Needs finding identifies the problem before choosing a solution; design inputs turn the need into measurable, testable specifications.
Risk analysis identifies hazards, estimates severity and probability, and adds mitigations; ISO 14971 is the international standard for medical device risk management.
Human factors and usability testing with real users reduce use-related hazards.
Verification checks that the design meets its specifications; validation checks that it meets the user need in the intended environment.
Design control links needs, specifications, outputs, verification and validation through a design history file, design reviews and change management.
Regulatory requirements and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria, NAFDAC regulates medical devices and COREN registers engineers.

en.title: Rehabilitation and assistive technology
en.short: Prostheses, orthoses, wheelchairs, walking aids, communication devices, fitting, EMG, FES and access.

sections.heading: Devices
sections.text:
Rehabilitation engineering applies engineering, including biomechanics and electronics, to help people with impaired movement or communication. A prosthesis replaces a missing body part; an orthosis supports, aligns or corrects a body segment. Wheelchairs, walking aids and augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices are assistive technology. Mechanics matter: a prosthesis needs a stable socket, load transfer and a knee or ankle matching the user’s gait; an orthosis must control motion without pressure injury. A wheelchair should fit seat width, depth and back height; wheels, castors and brakes affect propulsion and safety.

Example: a 100 kg wheelchair and user climb a 1:12 ramp. Ignoring friction, extra push along the slope is weight × rise ÷ slope length ≈ 100 × 9.81 × 1 ÷ 12.04 ≈ 82 N. Steeper ramps need more force.

sections.heading: Fitting and outcomes
sections.text: User-centred design starts with the person’s tasks, environment and preferences, not only the impairment. Fitting checks alignment, comfort, skin pressure, control and safety; it is done with the user and carers. Outcome measurement uses valid, repeatable tests, such as gait speed, walking distance, pain, function scores and satisfaction, before and after fitting. Evidence guides changes and compares devices.

sections.heading: EMG and FES
sections.text: Electromyography (EMG) records electrical activity from muscles. Surface electrodes are non-invasive; needle electrodes are clinical. EMG can trigger powered prostheses or assess muscle control. Functional electrical stimulation (FES) applies small current pulses to nerves or muscles to produce movement, such as lifting a dropped foot or opening a hand. It needs intact nerve and muscle, careful placement and clinical supervision; fatigue and skin effects limit use.

sections.heading: Access
sections.text: Access depends on cost, transport, repair, training and policy, not only performance. In low-resource settings, choose durable, repairable designs, local materials and manufacture, with spare parts and trained technicians. Universal design and accessible buildings, transport and information help everyone. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering practice; other countries have their own regulators, and standards and registration rules differ, so check current national requirements.

keyPoints: A prosthesis replaces a body part; an orthosis supports, aligns or corrects a segment.
User-centred fitting considers tasks, environment, comfort, skin pressure and safety with the user and carers.
Outcome measures such as gait speed and function scores should be valid and repeated before and after fitting.
EMG records muscle electrical activity; FES stimulates nerve or muscle to produce movement and needs clinical assessment.
For a ramp, extra push ≈ mass × g × rise ÷ slope length; a 100 kg user and wheelchair on 1:12 needs about 82 N ignoring friction.
Low-resource design should be durable, repairable and locally supported; design rules and registration differ by country, and in Nigeria COREN regulates engineering practice.

en.title: Clinical engineering and hospital safety
en.short: Managing hospital technology, electrical safety, incidents and user training.

sections.heading: Technology cycle
sections.text:
Clinical engineering is the hospital-based branch of biomedical engineering. It manages the technology cycle: acceptance testing before first use, inventory with unique identifiers, preventive maintenance (planned checks), calibration against a reference, repair, and replacement planning using age, failure history and spare-part risk. Acceptance testing confirms the device arrived and works as specified. Inventory records location, owner and service history. Preventive maintenance reduces sudden failure; calibration confirms measurement accuracy. Replacement planning avoids unsafe or unsupportable equipment. Codes and professional registration differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN registers engineers. Check local rules.

Example: 60 infusion pumps, preventive maintenance twice a year, 1 hour each, require 60 × 2 × 1 = 120 hours per year. If a technician has 1,800 productive hours per year, that is 120 ÷ 1,800 = 0.067, about 7% of the year.

sections.heading: Electrical safety
sections.text:
Mains-powered devices can pass small leakage current to earth through insulation and filters. Protective earthing gives fault current a low-resistance path so a fuse or breaker trips. The patient environment is the area around the patient where contact with equipment is likely. There, extra care is needed because catheters and electrodes can carry current directly to the heart; this is microshock risk. Leakage current is measured with a safety analyser. The IEC 60601 series is the international family of standards for medical electrical equipment; national editions and limits vary.

Formula: I = V ÷ R. Example: 230 V across 1,000 Ω gives 230 ÷ 1,000 = 0.23 A = 230 mA. Body resistance varies widely, so this is illustrative, not a safety threshold.

sections.heading: Incidents and training
sections.text: When equipment is linked to harm, preserve it, record settings, gather witness accounts and check maintenance and training records. A root cause analysis asks why the event happened and what system failed, not who to blame. Train clinical users on correct use, alarms and cleaning. Work with clinicians: engineers join ward rounds, safety committees and procurement. Document decisions.

keyPoints: The technology cycle runs from acceptance testing and inventory through preventive maintenance, calibration and repair to replacement planning; codes and registration differ by country, and COREN registers engineers in Nigeria.
Preventive maintenance and calibration protect accuracy and reduce sudden failure, while replacement planning uses age, failure history and spare-part risk.
Protective earthing gives fault current a low-resistance path, while leakage current is the small current flowing to earth.
Microshock risk is higher in the patient environment because electrodes and catheters can carry current to the heart.
Ohm’s law, I = V ÷ R, estimates current from voltage and resistance; body resistance varies, so it is illustrative only.
Incident investigation should preserve evidence, find system causes and improve training and procedures.

en.title: Medical device regulation and standards
en.short: How the FDA, EU MDR and NAFDAC classify and control devices, with ISO standards and post-market duties.

sections.heading: Risk classification
sections.text: A medical device is an article used for diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, treatment or alleviation of disease or injury, not mainly by pharmacological action. Regulators classify by risk. The US FDA uses Class I, II and III, with general controls, special controls and generally premarket approval. The EU MDR uses Class I, IIa, IIb and III, with notified bodies required above Class I. Nigeria’s NAFDAC registers devices on a risk basis; exact categories and fees change, so check current guidance.

sections.heading: Standards and evidence
sections.text: Standards supply evidence. ISO 13485 sets quality management system requirements. ISO 14971 sets risk management: identify hazards, estimate and control risk. The IEC 60601 series covers safety and essential performance of medical electrical equipment. Conformity assessment is the check that the device meets the rules, using the quality system, technical file, tests and clinical evaluation. Clinical evaluation is assessment of clinical evidence for safety and performance. Labelling covers instructions for use, symbols, warnings and a unique device identifier.

sections.heading: Market pathways
sections.text: Market pathways differ. In the US, many Class II devices use 510(k) premarket notification, showing substantial equivalence to a legally marketed device; Class III generally needs premarket approval. In the EU, the MDR requires CE marking, technical documentation and, above Class I, a notified body. In Nigeria, NAFDAC registration is needed before a device can be imported or sold. Each market also imposes its own labelling and post-market duties; one country’s approval is not automatically accepted elsewhere.

sections.heading: After sale
sections.text: Post-market surveillance (PMS) is ongoing review of real-world performance after sale: complaints, adverse event reporting, trend analysis, corrective action and recalls. Case: a firm plans a powered infusion pump. It builds an ISO 13485 system, uses ISO 14971 for hazards such as over-infusion, tests to IEC 60601, writes a clinical evaluation, prepares labels and sets up PMS. It checks the FDA route in the US, the MDR class and notified body in the EU, and NAFDAC registration in Nigeria. Rules and fees change, so confirm with official guidance.

keyPoints: Risk classification decides how much evidence and control a device needs, and the class names differ between the US FDA, EU MDR and Nigeria’s NAFDAC.
ISO 13485 covers the quality management system; ISO 14971 covers risk management; IEC 60601 covers electrical safety and essential performance.
Conformity assessment combines quality system evidence, technical files, testing and clinical evaluation.
In the US, many Class II devices use 510(k) and Class III generally uses premarket approval; the EU MDR uses CE marking and often a notified body; Nigeria requires NAFDAC registration.
Labelling and post-market surveillance are continuing legal duties, not optional extras.
Always check the current official guidance because classifications, fees and procedures change by country and year.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and COREN
en.short: Registration, codes of ethics, conflicts, whistleblowing and data protection in biomedical engineering.

sections.heading: Registration and regulation
sections.text: Engineering is regulated by law in many countries. In Nigeria, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN) registers engineers and regulates engineering practice. Comparable bodies include the Engineering Council in the United Kingdom, the Engineering Council of South Africa (ECSA), the Engineers Board of Kenya (EBK) and state licensing boards in the United States, with examinations from the National Council of Examiners for Engineering and Surveying (NCEES). The title 'engineer' is protected in some countries but not all. Requirements, fees and renewal rules differ, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Duties and codes
sections.text: An engineer’s first duty is to public safety, health and welfare. In biomedical engineering this includes patients who use devices and staff who operate them. Duties to employers include competent work, honesty and confidentiality, but loyalty never justifies hiding a hazard. Codes of ethics require competence: work only within your training and experience. Continuing professional development (CPD) keeps knowledge current. Record decisions and be willing to say 'I do not know'.

sections.heading: Conflicts, whistleblowing and data
sections.text: A conflict of interest is a personal interest that could bias professional judgement, such as a shareholding in a supplier. Disclose it and manage it. Whistleblowing is reporting unsafe or illegal practice. Use internal channels first where they work, keep records, and escalate to the regulator if needed. Data protection means handling patient data lawfully, securely and only for the stated purpose; laws differ by country. Research ethics requires ethics committee approval, informed consent, honest data and no fabrication.

sections.heading: Case discussion
sections.text: Amina, a biomedical engineer in a Nigerian hospital, finds a ventilator alarm limit changed without documentation. She records the setting, tells the clinical engineering manager and asks for the device to be withdrawn for checks. She does not share patient details. If the manager ignores the risk, she escalates to the hospital safety committee and, where required, the regulator.

keyPoints: COREN regulates engineering in Nigeria; comparable bodies exist elsewhere.
Public safety and patient welfare come before employer loyalty.
Work within your competence and keep CPD records.
Disclose conflicts of interest and manage them.
Report unsafe practice through proper channels; protect patient data.
