Research needs ethics approval, consent and honest reporting.

en.title: Research methods and the final-year project
en.short: Framing a question, reviewing literature, methods, sampling, ethics, data and reporting a final-year project.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text: A research question is the single question your project answers. It should name the population, the exposure or intervention, the outcome and the setting, and be answerable with your time and resources. A literature review is a structured search and critical reading of existing work. It shows what is known, what is disputed and where a gap remains. Cite every source you use.

sections.heading: Methods and sampling
sections.text: Quantitative methods collect numbers and test hypotheses with statistics. Qualitative methods explore experiences, meanings and reasons. Mixed methods combine both. Sampling means choosing participants from a defined population; the sampling frame is the list you draw from. Probability sampling gives each listed unit a known chance of selection. Non-probability sampling is quicker but limits generalisation. Measurement should be valid (it measures the intended idea) and reliable (it gives consistent results). Case: Amina, a student in Kano, Nigeria, times patients before and after a new malaria test queue and interviews staff about the change.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text: Ethics approval is needed before collecting data from people or their records. Informed consent means explaining the purpose, risks, benefits and the right to withdraw. Protect confidentiality, anonymise data and store files securely. Rules differ by country: in Nigeria, check the National Health Research Ethics Committee guidance and your institutional committee. A data management plan states what you will collect, how you will name and back up files, who may access them and how long you keep them. Never fabricate or alter data.

sections.heading: Proposal and report
sections.text: A proposal is the plan submitted before work begins. It usually has a title, background, question, aims, methods, ethics, timeline, budget and references. Your supervisor helps narrow the scope and spot risks; keep a logbook. The final report usually follows abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Report negative results honestly. In your presentation, use clear slides, rehearse and state your limitations.

keyPoints: A research question names the population, exposure or intervention, outcome and setting.
A literature review shows what is known, what is disputed and where a gap remains.
Quantitative methods use numbers; qualitative methods explore meanings; mixed methods combine both.
Probability sampling gives each listed unit a known chance of selection.
Ethics approval and informed consent come before data collection; rules differ by country.
A data management plan covers collection, naming, backup, access and retention.

en.title: Advanced biomechanics and mechanobiology
en.short: Finite-strain continuum models, tissue anisotropy, mechanobiology and validated finite element analysis.

sections.heading: Continuum framework
sections.text:
Continuum mechanics treats tissue as a continuous material. The deformation gradient F records local stretch; J = det F is the volume ratio. Cauchy stress σ acts on deformed area; first Piola stress P acts on original area. Soft tissues sustain large finite strain and are nearly incompressible, so small-strain theory is inadequate. Hard tissues are stiffer but anisotropic and time-dependent.

Example: a tendon strip 100 mm long is stretched to 103 mm. λ = 103 ÷ 100 = 1.03. Green-Lagrange strain E = (λ² − 1) ÷ 2 = (1.0609 − 1) ÷ 2 = 0.03045, about 3.0%.

sections.heading: Anisotropic tissue models
sections.text: Collagen fibres, elastin and mineral crystals make tissue direction-dependent. A constitutive model links deformation to stress through a strain-energy function W. For a hyperelastic solid, P = ∂W/∂F and σ = (1/J) P F^T. Anisotropy uses fibre directions and fibre recruitment, often as an isotropic matrix plus fibre families. Tendon, ligament and arterial wall are modelled as fibre-reinforced. Cortical bone is treated as orthotropic or transversely isotropic. Parameters must come from independent tests, and tension-compression asymmetry is common.

sections.heading: Mechanobiology
sections.text: Mechanobiology studies how mechanical cues change cell behaviour. Cells sense stretch, shear stress, pressure and matrix stiffness through integrins, ion channels and the cytoskeleton. Mechanotransduction converts these cues into biochemical signals that alter gene expression, migration, proliferation and matrix synthesis. Endothelial cells respond to blood flow shear; osteocytes respond to fluid flow in bone; fibroblasts remodel collagen under tension. Bone adapts to habitual loading, described by Wolff’s law. Responses depend on loading history and cell type.

sections.heading: Computing and validation
sections.text: Finite element analysis divides an organ or tissue region into elements and solves equilibrium numerically. Musculoskeletal models need muscle forces, joint contact and constraints; cardiovascular models need inlet flow, outlet pressure and wall prestress. Mesh convergence is checked by refining until outputs change little. Verification checks the code; validation compares predictions with independent experiments, for example force-displacement tests or pressure-diameter curves. Calibration and validation data must be separate.

keyPoints: Soft tissues require finite-strain continuum mechanics; λ = L/L0 and E = (λ² − 1) ÷ 2 measure stretch and Green-Lagrange strain.
For hyperelastic tissue, first Piola stress is P = ∂W/∂F and Cauchy stress is σ = (1/J) P F^T.
Anisotropy comes from collagen and mineral orientation, so fibre direction and tension-compression asymmetry must be included.
Mechanotransduction converts stretch, shear and stiffness into biochemical signals that change cell behaviour.
Finite element models need mesh convergence checks and realistic boundary conditions.
Validation compares model predictions with independent experiments; calibration data must not be reused for validation.

en.title: Advanced biomedical signal and image analysis
en.short: Time-frequency and wavelet methods, adaptive filtering, BSS, machine learning, registration and deep segmentation.

sections.heading: Time-frequency and wavelets
sections.text:
An EEG or ECG signal is non-stationary: its frequency content changes over time. The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) applies a windowed Fourier transform, trading time against frequency resolution. A short window gives good time resolution, a long window good frequency resolution.

The wavelet transform uses short windows at high frequencies and long windows at low frequencies, giving a time-scale view. The discrete wavelet transform splits a signal into approximation and detail coefficients by filtering and downsampling, then repeats the split on the approximation. Wavelets suit spikes and transients; the STFT suits steady rhythms.

sections.heading: Adaptive filtering and BSS
sections.text:
An adaptive filter changes its coefficients as data arrive, minimising an error signal. Least mean squares (LMS) updates the weights by w_new = w + μ·e·x, where μ is the step size, e the error and x the input vector; recursive least squares converges faster at higher cost. Adaptive filters cancel mains interference.

Blind source separation (BSS) recovers sources from mixed recordings without knowing the mixing. Independent component analysis (ICA) assumes the sources are statistically independent and non-Gaussian, and can remove eye blinks from EEG. It needs at least as many channels as sources.

sections.heading: Learning and segmentation
sections.text:
Classifiers map features to labels: train on one set, tune on a validation set, report on untouched test data. Deep learning learns the features itself. A convolutional neural network (CNN) applies learned filters; U-Net, an encoder-decoder CNN with skip connections, is a common segmentation architecture.

Image registration finds a transform that aligns two images, rigid (rotation and translation) or non-rigid (deformable), by maximising a similarity measure such as mutual information.

sections.heading: Evaluation and translation
sections.text:
Report sensitivity, specificity, Dice score (2|A∩B| ÷ (|A|+|B|)) and confidence intervals, not accuracy alone on imbalanced data. Reproducibility needs fixed data splits, documented preprocessing, released code and recorded random seeds.

Clinical translation needs external validation on other scanners and sites, plus regulatory approval. Requirements differ by country, so check the current national regulator, for example the FDA in the United States or NAFDAC in Nigeria.

keyPoints: The STFT trades time resolution against frequency resolution; wavelets use short windows at high frequencies.
LMS weight update: w_new = w + μ·e·x, with step size μ controlling speed and stability.
ICA separates independent, non-Gaussian sources and needs at least as many channels as sources.
U-Net is an encoder-decoder CNN with skip connections used for image segmentation.
Registration maximises a similarity measure over a rigid or deformable transform.
Report Dice score and confidence intervals on held-out data, and validate externally before clinical use.

en.title: Tissue engineering and regenerative medicine
en.short: Scaffolds, cell sources, growth factors, bioreactors, vascularisation, regulation and repair cases.

sections.heading: Scaffolds and cells
sections.text:
A scaffold is a temporary extracellular matrix: it gives shape, pores for cell migration and mass transport, and mechanical cues. Design balances porosity, pore size, degradation rate and stiffness. Fabrication includes freeze-drying, salt leaching, electrospinning and 3D printing. Example: a 1 cm³ scaffold with 90% porosity has 0.9 cm³ pore volume; at 20 million cells/mL, the seed dose is 18 million cells.

Cell sources are autologous (patient), allogeneic (donor) or xenogeneic (animal). Stem cells include adult mesenchymal stromal cells and induced pluripotent cells; embryonic stem cells raise ethical issues. Expansion and differentiation need control.

sections.heading: Signals and bioreactors
sections.text:
Growth factors are proteins that instruct cells: VEGF supports blood vessels, TGF-β family members regulate cartilage and matrix, BMPs drive bone formation. They need dose, timing and local delivery; uncontrolled doses can cause side effects.

Bioreactors control temperature, pH, oxygen and waste removal, and apply mechanical conditioning: perfusion shear, cyclic stretch or compression. Mechanical cues influence matrix production and alignment, but parameters are tissue-specific.

sections.heading: Vascularisation and integration
sections.text: Cells beyond about 100 to 200 µm from a capillary rely on diffusion and become hypoxic; a standard estimate, not a fixed rule. Thick constructs need preformed channels or rapid new blood vessels. Host integration depends on immune response, scaffold degradation, mechanical match and stable blood supply. In vivo, the scaffold should be replaced by host matrix.

sections.heading: Regulation and cases
sections.text:
Regulation differs by country. In the United States the FDA regulates human cells and tissues; in the European Union advanced therapy medicinal products follow EMA pathways; in Nigeria NAFDAC regulates medicines and devices. Rules cover consent, good manufacturing practice, sterility and tumourigenicity. Ethics committees review embryo-derived cells and donor consent. Check current guidance.

Skin: cultured keratinocytes and dermal scaffolds close wounds. Cartilage: chondrocytes or mesenchymal cells in hydrogels with loading. Bone: porous ceramics with BMPs and osteogenic cells. Blood vessels: tubular scaffolds seeded with endothelial and smooth muscle cells, conditioned in pulsatile bioreactors.

keyPoints: Scaffolds must balance porosity, pore size, degradation and mechanical match to guide cells and mass transport.
Autologous, allogeneic and stem cell sources differ in availability, immune risk and ethical review.
Growth factors such as VEGF, TGF-β family members and BMPs need controlled dose, timing and delivery.
Bioreactors supply nutrients and mechanical cues; conditioning parameters are tissue-specific.
Diffusion limits vascularisation, so thick constructs need channels or rapid new blood vessels for host integration.
Regulation and ethics differ by country; check the official regulator and ethics committee before translation.

en.title: Research methods for a biomedical engineering dissertation
en.short: Designing a master’s dissertation: literature, theory, protocol, analysis, ethics and planning.

sections.heading: Question to protocol
sections.text:
A master’s dissertation starts with a gap stated in one sentence. A critical literature review compares methods, samples and findings, and shows where evidence is weak or missing; it is not a list of papers.

From it build a theory: define each construct, say how it will be measured, and draw a conceptual framework. Then write a testable hypothesis, or a focused research question for qualitative work. The protocol records aim, design, participants, inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size justification, analysis plan, ethics and timeline. Example: a Lagos student testing a low-cost pulse oximeter against a hospital device states the reference standard, patient group and agreement analysis plan before collecting data.

sections.heading: Quantitative and qualitative
sections.text:
Quantitative designs test hypotheses with numbers, using experiments, surveys or record reviews; analysis may be descriptive or inferential. Qualitative designs explore experience and meaning through interviews, focus groups or observation; analysis often uses thematic coding.

Mixed methods combine both and must say how the strands connect. Pre-specify the analysis so results are not chosen after seeing data. For qualitative work, show trustworthiness: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text:
Ethics approval is required before recruitment. In Nigeria, a Health Research Ethics Committee accredited by the National Health Research Ethics Committee reviews health studies; other countries differ, so check your institution. Informed consent, confidentiality and protection of vulnerable groups are core.

Data protection law differs: Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 governs personal data. Anonymise where possible, store data securely, limit access, and state retention and destruction. For devices, include electrical and biological safety risks.

sections.heading: Writing and planning
sections.text:
Write in IMRaD form: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion. A critical review weighs evidence; it does not list papers. Keep a decision log and cite primary sources.

Plan backwards from submission: milestones, a Gantt chart, resources, buffer for ethics delays, and a risk register. Publication follows the same discipline: target a journal, follow its author guidelines, declare conflicts, and expect peer review.

keyPoints: A critical review compares evidence and identifies a gap; it is not a list of papers.
Define constructs and a conceptual framework before stating a testable hypothesis.
Pre-specify the analysis plan for quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods.
Ethics approval and data protection compliance come before recruitment.
Plan milestones, resources and buffer time for ethics and recruitment delays.
Write in IMRaD and cite primary sources; publication follows journal guidelines and peer review.
